1	# Roofs by style
2	
3	Roofs are where builds go wrong: flat caps, lumpy hips, stairs facing the wrong way. Don't place roof blocks by
4	hand. Choose a **style** and a few options, and the tool builds it. It gets stair facing, half and corner shapes
5	right at hips and valleys, closes steep faces, fills gable walls, and adds verges, eaves, ridge caps, dormers, a
6	pediment, chimneys and a tower. It works over a rectangle or a union of rectangles (L, T and U plans) and leaves the
7	inside hollow as an attic.
8	
9	```
10	mcd roof build.nbt --detect                                   # where is the eave, what is the footprint?
11	mcd roof build.nbt out.nbt --style hip --pitch 45 --eave cornice --material deepslate_tiles --ridge crest
12	mcd roof build.nbt out.nbt --spec roof.json                   # the same options as JSON
13	mcd compare build.nbt out.nbt --front n                       # look at it
14	```
15	```js
16	import { roof, reroof, detectEave } from "<plugin>/tools/src/build.mjs";
17	roof(g, [[2, 2, 14, 10], [2, 11, 8, 16]], "hip", { y: 6, material: "deepslate_tile", eave: "cornice" });   // new build: y = wall top + 1
18	reroof(g, { style: "mansard", pitch: "steep", pediment: "north" });                                      // existing build
19	```
20	
21	## Presets first
22	
23	A builder's own parameter choices for `mcd roof` kept producing the same failure: a low pitch, no overhang, no
24	ridge, and the roof in the wall material, so the roof read as a heavy lid that merged with the walls. **Start from a
25	preset.** Each one is good by construction and scales to the footprint:
26	- the pitch scales with the span;
27	- the overhang is 1 cell, or 2 on spans of 15 or more;
28	- dormer and chimney counts scale with the length;
29	- on walls of two storeys or less, the roof is never taller than the walls (cottage, shop and granary are steep by
30	  design).
31	
32	```
33	mcd roof build.nbt out.nbt --preset civic                     # flags override any preset field:
34	mcd roof build.nbt out.nbt --preset townhouse --material dark_oak --front e
35	```
36	```js
37	roof(g, rects, "cottage", { y });            // a preset name works as the style
38	reroof(g, { preset: "civic" });
39	```
40	
41	| preset | the roof | good for |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| `cottage` | steep gable, `spruce-shingle` palette with dark oak verges, flared eaves, slab ridge, one chimney at a gable end | houses, cottages, rural buildings |
44	| `shop` | steep front gable (gable end to the street), `spruce-shingle` with spruce verges; side dormers on spans of 13+ | shopfronts, market buildings |
45	| `townhouse` | `dark-slate` mansard with dormers on the street face, stone cornice with dentils, iron-bar crest | row houses, Second Empire blocks |
46	| `civic` | 45-degree hip in the `slate` palette, quartz dentil cornice, a quartz pediment over the front | banks, halls, offices |
47	| `temple` | low gable to the front, `red-tile` palette, quartz raking cornice and tympanum, the cornice carried across the pediment's base | colonnades, porticos, museums |
48	| `granary` (`industrial`) | tall `slate` gable with a louvred monitor along the middle of the ridge | barns, granaries, workshops |
49	| `modern` (`flat-parapet-modern`) | parapet, smooth stone coping, a slim cornice without dentils, iron-bar rooftop rail | modern and commercial blocks |
50	| `barn` | gambrel along the long axis (break at 40% of the span, 1.5 then 0.5), `barn-red`, quartz barge boards, 2 dormers per long side (3 on 18+), a lantern cupola on the ridge | barns, stables, farm sheds |
51	| `teahouse` (`pagoda`) | low dutch gable, pitch 0.67, upturned eave corners with rafter tails, dark glazed tiles, stone ridge; the roof stays under 0.6 of the wall height | tea houses, shrines, East Asian pavilions |
52	| `tower-cap` | cone at 2.75:1 with a concave flare and a finial, a dormer on towers 7+ wide (override `material: copper` for a verdigris cap) | wizard towers, keeps, turrets |
53	| `lantern-cap` | shallow cone (1.25:1) with a ring course and finial | lighthouse lanterns, gazebos, bell cupolas |
54	| `church` (`stave`) | three stacked, steeper roofs (1, 1.5, 2) with a wall band and a window row between, dragon ridge ends, dark shingle mix | stave churches, pagodas, tiered halls |
55	| `workshop` | sawtooth: a row of sheds (one per 5 cells) with glazed north faces, `copper` in gap-free stairs and slabs | workshops, factories, studios |
56	| `desert` | flat sandstone deck, quartz coping, a wind tower | desert markets, adobe, flat-roofed villages |
57	| `cafe` | flat cantilever deck, overhang N2 S1 E1 W1, thin quartz fascia, spruce soffit, a vent stack | glass cafes, modern shopfronts with a canopy |
58	
59	**Contrast** applies to presets and plain styles alike. If the roof material's measured tone is too close to the
60	dominant wall block (tone distance below 0.3, families.mjs colours), the preset's alternate material is used (or the
61	first that clears from the slate, spruce-shingle, dark-slate and red-tile palettes, dark oak, quartz, mud brick), and the result
62	`notes` say so. `contrast: false` (`--no-contrast`) keeps the material, for example a concept that wants dark slate
63	on dark walls. Overhang is always at least 1 unless you pass `overhang: 0`.
64	
65	## Pick the preset by building type
66	
67	Look the building up in the table above and use its preset on the first `mcd roof` call. Do not start from `--style`.
68	Quick map: house, cottage -> `cottage`; shopfront -> `shop`; row house -> `townhouse`; hall, bank -> `civic`; colonnade ->
69	`temple`; barn, stable -> `barn`; tea house, pagoda, shrine -> `teahouse`; round or square tower -> `tower-cap`; lighthouse
70	lantern -> `lantern-cap`; church, tiered hall -> `church`; factory, workshop -> `workshop`; desert, adobe -> `desert`; flat
71	cafe, modern block -> `cafe` or `modern`. `roof-review.mjs` has `SIZE_BUDGET` (wall courses and roof/wall ratio per type).
72	
73	## Palettes: a roof is never one flat plane
74	
75	`material` takes a **palette**, a single block (mixed automatically with two same-family neighbours) or your own
76	`{ mix: [[block, weight], ...], eave, ridge, verge, gradient, rows }`. Each palette is a weighted mix of 3+ visibly different
77	blocks, a darker eave course, a distinct ridge and verge. The default (no `material`) is `slate`, never one near-black
78	block. `--texture <palette>` / `texture: false` (one flat block: needs a reason, see below).
79	
80	| palette | mix | use for |
81	|---|---|---|
82	| `slate` (default) | cobbled deepslate, deepslate tile, polished deepslate; blackstone-brick eave, stone-brick ridge | civic, general |
83	| `dark-slate` | deepslate tile with cobbled, blackstone and cracked-tile accents | townhouses, dark Gothic |
84	| `spruce-shingle` | spruce, dark oak, mangrove; dark oak eave, birch verge | cottages, shops |
85	| `red-tile` | brick, granite, polished granite, mangrove; mud-brick eave, quartz verge | temples, Mediterranean |
86	| `barn-red` | mangrove, brick, dark oak; dark oak eave, quartz verge | barns |
87	| `copper` | weathered and oxidized cut copper in rows; exposed eave, cut-copper ridge | towers, workshops, coastal |
88	| `dark-glazed` | deepslate tile, cobbled deepslate, blackstone brick; quartz ridge | East Asian tiles |
89	| `sandstone-deck` | smooth sandstone, cut sandstone, sandstone; quartz coping | flat desert roofs |
90	
91	## Guard rails and `--dry-run`
92	
93	Run `mcd roof in.nbt --preset <name> --dry-run` FIRST (a dry run writes nothing). It prints the roof report (wall and roof
94	height, ratio and its cap, overhang, tones, breaks) and every warning with a fix. Fix each warning, then run it for real. The
95	same warnings come back after a real run in `notes`, and `--strict` exits 2 on any.
96	
97	| warning | meaning | fix |
98	|---|---|---|
99	| `ROOF_CONTRAST_OFF` | `--no-contrast` | drop it; choose a palette 0.3+ in tone from the walls |
100	| `ROOF_NO_OVERHANG` | a side has overhang 0 | overhang 1 (2 on spans of 15+); shorten the walls to fit a size cap |
101	| `ROOF_SINGLE_MATERIAL` | under 3 visible tones or `--texture none` | a palette or a 3+ block mix |
102	| `ROOF_TOO_TALL` | roof / wall ratio over the cap (0.6 on walls of 5 or less, 1.0 up to 9, 1.8 for cottage, barn, cone, church) | lower the pitch, raise the walls, a steep-by-design preset |
103	| `ROOF_LOW_PITCH` | pitch under 0.5 | pitch 0.5+ (0.67 only with `eave: upturned`) |
104	| `ROOF_BIG_PLANE` | an unbroken slope 10+ long | dormers, chimney, cross-gable, monitor, or gambrel / mansard |
105	| `ROOF_NO_RIDGE` | bare ridge seam | `ridge: slab` (crest on a mansard) |
106	| `ROOF_BLACK_LID` | near-black roof barely lighter than the walls | slate grey or a warm palette |
107	| `ROOF_DORMER_DROPPED` | a dormer did not fit | a longer face (7+), or another break |
108	
109	**The bypass rule.** Never bypass a guard rail (`--no-contrast`, `--overhang 0`, `--texture none`, a pitch under 0.5)
110	without `--why "<reason that cites the concept image>"`, for example `--why "concept: black tiled roof on black timber walls"`.
111	Without a reason the tool refuses (CLI) or warns (library); with one it records the reason as a look note. "To fit the size
112	cap" is not a reason: shorten the walls. Forms with no eave by design (sawtooth, dome) are exempt automatically.
113	
114	## Forms beyond a pitched plane
115	
116	`--style cone | dome | onion | tiered | sawtooth` (or the presets above) build curved, stacked and glazed roofs:
117	`cone` (`pitch`, `lean`, `finial`, `dormer`), `dome`/`onion` (`drum`, `ribs`, finial; radius under 4 falls back to a cone),
118	`tiered` (`tiers`, `skirt`, `inset`, `band`, `pitches`), `sawtooth` (`bays`, `glaze`). `eave: upturned` lifts the corners of a
119	dutch gable or hip like a pagoda; `overhang` may be `{north, south, east, west}`; `maxHeight` caps the roof in courses (with no
120	explicit pitch the roof is capped at its ratio cap). `mcd render --closeups` includes a roof close-up tile so the texture is visible.
121	`examples/roofs/regression.png` shows the eight reference cases (`node examples/roofs/regression.mjs`).
122	
123	`examples/roofs/presets.png` shows every preset on a small 9x7 shop and a 23x17 civic block
124	(`node examples/roofs/presets.mjs`).
125	
126	## Styles (the raw options)
127	
128	`examples/roofs/gallery.png` shows every style on the same L-plan house (`node examples/roofs/gallery.mjs`).
129	
130	| style | what it is | good for |
131	|---|---|---|
132	| `gable` | two slopes per wing; ridges along each wing's long side, cross-gables meeting in valleys; gable walls filled with the wall block | cottages, barns, row houses (`ridgeAxis` to turn the ridge) |
133	| `hip` | slopes on every side; true hips (outer stairs) and valleys (inner stairs) on any rectilinear plan | villas, civic buildings, anything seen from all sides |
134	| `pyramid` | a hip that comes to points; a square plan gives a single peak | pavilions, towers |
135	| `mansard` | a steep lower slope (`pitch`, `lower` cells wide) under a shallow upper one (`upperPitch`, default half) | French or Second Empire roofs, a full storey in the roof, dormers |
136	| `gambrel` | gable wings with two pitches | barns, Dutch colonial |
137	| `flat-parapet` | a flat deck, a parapet (`parapet` courses) of the wall block, and slab coping | shops, offices, modern buildings |
138	| `shed` | one slope (the `low` side), with the high side walled | lean-tos, extensions, industrial buildings |
139	| `dutch-gable` | a hip with small gablets set back at the ridge ends (`inset`) | farmhouses, East Asian roofs |
140	
141	## Options
142	
143	- **`pitch`**:
144	  - `half`: slab steps, about 27°
145	  - `45`: stairs, 1:1
146	  - `steep`: stairs with full blocks, 2:1
147	  - `very-steep`: 3:1
148	  - or any number (rise per cell)
149	
150	  Eaves never drop more than one course per cell, so a steep roof does not swallow the top of the wall.
151	- **`overhang`** 0–2 (default 1). **`eave`**:
152	  - `plain`
153	  - `flared`: a half-pitch kick at the eave
154	  - `cornice`: a course of upside-down `trim` stairs under the eave, with dentils of alternating `trim` blocks under that
155	
156	  `soffit: true` (or a material) puts top slabs under a plain overhang.
157	- **Materials**:
158	  - `material` (the roof; any form of the name works: `deepslate_tiles`, `deepslate_tile`, `spruce`)
159	  - `trim` (cornice, dentils, tower band)
160	  - `gable` (the gable-end wall; default: the walls' own block)
161	  - `verge` (the barge course over each gable end)
162	  - `hips` (the hip stairs)
163	  - `pattern: {material, every, offset}` (banded courses)
164	- **`ridge`**:
165	  - `slab` (default for 45° and steeper): a half slab on the ridge
166	  - `wall`: a joined wall
167	  - `crest`: joined iron bars, the Victorian ridge crest
168	  - `rods`: end rods every other cell
169	  - `none`
170	  - or any block
171	- **`dormers`**: `{face, count | every, style: gable|shed|eyebrow, width (3), height (2), window, wall}`. Dormers are
172	  placed symmetrically on that face of the largest wing, keep clear of hip ends and the pediment, and step down or
173	  drop out where the main roof doesn't rise over them within four rows (so they never tunnel through it).
174	- **`pediment`**: `{face, width (55% of the face), pitch (45), tympanum, cornice (raking cornice material), oculus
175	  (true), depth}`, or just `"north"`. This is a classical cross-gable over the front half of that face, with its
176	  gable filled with `tympanum`, a raking cornice, and a small round window in the middle.
177	- **`chimneys`**: `[{at: [x,z], size, material, rise}]`. A chimney rises `rise` (2) above the roof top. A 1x1 chimney
178	  gets a smoking campfire on top, and bigger ones get slab caps.
179	- **`tower`**: `{at: [x,z], size (n or [w,d]), height (above the roof top), top: lantern|spire|cap, material}`. This
180	  is a hollow shaft through the roof with a band and small openings near the top, finished with one of:
181	  - `lantern`: corner posts, iron-bar railings, a hanging lantern, a small pyramid cap and a lightning-rod finial
182	  - `spire`: a 3:1 pyramid
183	  - `cap`: slab coping
184	- **`monitor`** (gable styles): a louvred vent along the middle 60% of the ridge. **`gableCornice`**: the cornice
185	  also runs across the gable ends (the base of a pediment). **`dentils: false`**: a slim cornice. **`rail`**
186	  (flat-parapet): iron bars along the coping.
187	- **`keep`**: `[{from:[x,y,z], to:[x,y,z]}]`, cells never written or removed (a chimney or tower you want to keep).
188	  Functional cells (redstone, doors and the rest) are always protected. `grow` (default true) grows the grid to fit
189	  overhangs and height; the result's `shift` says how far everything moved.
190	
191	## Re-roofing an existing build
192	
193	`reroof` and `mcd roof` work in three steps:
194	1. **Find the walls.** Tall columns are walls; the holes between them are filled to get the plan.
195	2. **Find the eave.** Each perimeter column's wall top is its highest solid with a mostly solid column beneath
196	   (stairs and slabs at the top count as roof). The eave is the most common wall top.
197	3. **Find the footprint.** Columns that reach the eave band form it, so a low porch drops out. It is cleaned up
198	   (one-cell notches filled, one-cell pilasters and buttresses dropped), split into rectangles, and keep boxes are
199	   cut out.
200	
201	Then it removes everything above the eave over the footprint (+3 for old overhangs), plus old eave stairs and slabs,
202	and builds the style. Check `--detect` first. If the footprint is wrong, pass `--footprint x0,z0,x1,z1;...` and
203	`--y`.
204	
205	## Choosing a roof that matches a concept
206	
207	- **Roof height**: a steep hip over a 16-wide plan rises 16 blocks, which is taller than most concepts show. For
208	  "steep slate" on a wide building, use a **mansard** (`pitch: steep`, `lower: 3`): it reads as a steep roof from
209	  the street, and the shallow top holds the crest.
210	- **A front pediment** turns a plain roof into a civic one. Use `cornice` in an accent material (oak reads as gilt
211	  against slate) and `eave: cornice` on the main roof.
212	- **Towers** read best small. An elevator head is the shaft's front 4x5 and one storey above the roof, not the whole
213	  shaft.
214	
215	The worked example is `examples/roofs/deepslate.mjs`, which re-roofs Deepslate Holdings to match its concept.
216	`examples/roofs/deepslate-compare.png` shows the concept, before and after.

# Roofs by style

Roofs are where builds go wrong: flat caps, lumpy hips, stairs facing the wrong way. Don't place roof blocks by
hand. Choose a **style** and a few options, and the tool builds it. It gets stair facing, half and corner shapes
right at hips and valleys, closes steep faces, fills gable walls, and adds verges, eaves, ridge caps, dormers, a
pediment, chimneys and a tower. It works over a rectangle or a union of rectangles (L, T and U plans) and leaves the
inside hollow as an attic.

```
mcd roof build.nbt --detect                                   # where is the eave, what is the footprint?
mcd roof build.nbt out.nbt --style hip --pitch 45 --eave cornice --material deepslate_tiles --ridge crest
mcd roof build.nbt out.nbt --spec roof.json                   # the same options as JSON
mcd compare build.nbt out.nbt --front n                       # look at it
```
```js
import { roof, reroof, detectEave } from "<plugin>/tools/src/build.mjs";
roof(g, [[2, 2, 14, 10], [2, 11, 8, 16]], "hip", { y: 6, material: "deepslate_tile", eave: "cornice" });   // new build: y = wall top + 1
reroof(g, { style: "mansard", pitch: "steep", pediment: "north" });                                      // existing build
```

## Presets first

A builder's own parameter choices for `mcd roof` kept producing the same failure: a low pitch, no overhang, no
ridge, and the roof in the wall material, so the roof read as a heavy lid that merged with the walls. **Start from a
preset.** Each one is good by construction and scales to the footprint:
- the pitch scales with the span;
- the overhang is 1 cell, or 2 on spans of 15 or more;
- dormer and chimney counts scale with the length;
- on walls of two storeys or less, the roof is never taller than the walls (cottage, shop and granary are steep by
  design).

```
mcd roof build.nbt out.nbt --preset civic                     # flags override any preset field:
mcd roof build.nbt out.nbt --preset townhouse --material dark_oak --front e
```
```js
roof(g, rects, "cottage", { y });            // a preset name works as the style
reroof(g, { preset: "civic" });
```

| preset | the roof | good for |
|---|---|---|
| `cottage` | steep gable, `spruce-shingle` palette with dark oak verges, flared eaves, slab ridge, one chimney at a gable end | houses, cottages, rural buildings |
| `shop` | steep front gable (gable end to the street), `spruce-shingle` with spruce verges; side dormers on spans of 13+ | shopfronts, market buildings |
| `townhouse` | `dark-slate` mansard with dormers on the street face, stone cornice with dentils, iron-bar crest | row houses, Second Empire blocks |
| `civic` | 45-degree hip in the `slate` palette, quartz dentil cornice, a quartz pediment over the front | banks, halls, offices |
| `temple` | low gable to the front, `red-tile` palette, quartz raking cornice and tympanum, the cornice carried across the pediment's base | colonnades, porticos, museums |
| `granary` (`industrial`) | tall `slate` gable with a louvred monitor along the middle of the ridge | barns, granaries, workshops |
| `modern` (`flat-parapet-modern`) | parapet, smooth stone coping, a slim cornice without dentils, iron-bar rooftop rail | modern and commercial blocks |
| `barn` | gambrel along the long axis (break at 40% of the span, 1.5 then 0.5), `barn-red`, quartz barge boards, 2 dormers per long side (3 on 18+), a lantern cupola on the ridge | barns, stables, farm sheds |
| `teahouse` (`pagoda`) | low dutch gable, pitch 0.67, upturned eave corners with rafter tails, dark glazed tiles, stone ridge; the roof stays under 0.6 of the wall height | tea houses, shrines, East Asian pavilions |
| `tower-cap` | cone at 2.75:1 with a concave flare and a finial, a dormer on towers 7+ wide (override `material: copper` for a verdigris cap) | wizard towers, keeps, turrets |
| `lantern-cap` | shallow cone (1.25:1) with a ring course and finial | lighthouse lanterns, gazebos, bell cupolas |
| `church` (`stave`) | three stacked, steeper roofs (1, 1.5, 2) with a wall band and a window row between, dragon ridge ends, dark shingle mix | stave churches, pagodas, tiered halls |
| `workshop` | sawtooth: a row of sheds (one per 5 cells) with glazed north faces, `copper` in gap-free stairs and slabs | workshops, factories, studios |
| `desert` | flat sandstone deck, quartz coping, a wind tower | desert markets, adobe, flat-roofed villages |
| `cafe` | flat cantilever deck, overhang N2 S1 E1 W1, thin quartz fascia, spruce soffit, a vent stack | glass cafes, modern shopfronts with a canopy |

**Contrast** applies to presets and plain styles alike. If the roof material's measured tone is too close to the
dominant wall block (tone distance below 0.3, families.mjs colours), the preset's alternate material is used (or the
first that clears from the slate, spruce-shingle, dark-slate and red-tile palettes, dark oak, quartz, mud brick), and the result
`notes` say so. `contrast: false` (`--no-contrast`) keeps the material, for example a concept that wants dark slate
on dark walls. Overhang is always at least 1 unless you pass `overhang: 0`.

## Pick the preset by building type

Look the building up in the table above and use its preset on the first `mcd roof` call. Do not start from `--style`.
Quick map: house, cottage -> `cottage`; shopfront -> `shop`; row house -> `townhouse`; hall, bank -> `civic`; colonnade ->
`temple`; barn, stable -> `barn`; tea house, pagoda, shrine -> `teahouse`; round or square tower -> `tower-cap`; lighthouse
lantern -> `lantern-cap`; church, tiered hall -> `church`; factory, workshop -> `workshop`; desert, adobe -> `desert`; flat
cafe, modern block -> `cafe` or `modern`. `roof-review.mjs` has `SIZE_BUDGET` (wall courses and roof/wall ratio per type).

## Palettes: a roof is never one flat plane

`material` takes a **palette**, a single block (mixed automatically with two same-family neighbours) or your own
`{ mix: [[block, weight], ...], eave, ridge, verge, gradient, rows }`. Each palette is a weighted mix of 3+ visibly different
blocks, a darker eave course, a distinct ridge and verge. The default (no `material`) is `slate`, never one near-black
block. `--texture <palette>` / `texture: false` (one flat block: needs a reason, see below).

| palette | mix | use for |
|---|---|---|
| `slate` (default) | cobbled deepslate, deepslate tile, polished deepslate; blackstone-brick eave, stone-brick ridge | civic, general |
| `dark-slate` | deepslate tile with cobbled, blackstone and cracked-tile accents | townhouses, dark Gothic |
| `spruce-shingle` | spruce, dark oak, mangrove; dark oak eave, birch verge | cottages, shops |
| `red-tile` | brick, granite, polished granite, mangrove; mud-brick eave, quartz verge | temples, Mediterranean |
| `barn-red` | mangrove, brick, dark oak; dark oak eave, quartz verge | barns |
| `copper` | weathered and oxidized cut copper in rows; exposed eave, cut-copper ridge | towers, workshops, coastal |
| `dark-glazed` | deepslate tile, cobbled deepslate, blackstone brick; quartz ridge | East Asian tiles |
| `sandstone-deck` | smooth sandstone, cut sandstone, sandstone; quartz coping | flat desert roofs |

## Guard rails and `--dry-run`

Run `mcd roof in.nbt --preset <name> --dry-run` FIRST (a dry run writes nothing). It prints the roof report (wall and roof
height, ratio and its cap, overhang, tones, breaks) and every warning with a fix. Fix each warning, then run it for real. The
same warnings come back after a real run in `notes`, and `--strict` exits 2 on any.

| warning | meaning | fix |
|---|---|---|
| `ROOF_CONTRAST_OFF` | `--no-contrast` | drop it; choose a palette 0.3+ in tone from the walls |
| `ROOF_NO_OVERHANG` | a side has overhang 0 | overhang 1 (2 on spans of 15+); shorten the walls to fit a size cap |
| `ROOF_SINGLE_MATERIAL` | under 3 visible tones or `--texture none` | a palette or a 3+ block mix |
| `ROOF_TOO_TALL` | roof / wall ratio over the cap (0.6 on walls of 5 or less, 1.0 up to 9, 1.8 for cottage, barn, cone, church) | lower the pitch, raise the walls, a steep-by-design preset |
| `ROOF_LOW_PITCH` | pitch under 0.5 | pitch 0.5+ (0.67 only with `eave: upturned`) |
| `ROOF_BIG_PLANE` | an unbroken slope 10+ long | dormers, chimney, cross-gable, monitor, or gambrel / mansard |
| `ROOF_NO_RIDGE` | bare ridge seam | `ridge: slab` (crest on a mansard) |
| `ROOF_BLACK_LID` | near-black roof barely lighter than the walls | slate grey or a warm palette |
| `ROOF_DORMER_DROPPED` | a dormer did not fit | a longer face (7+), or another break |

**The bypass rule.** Never bypass a guard rail (`--no-contrast`, `--overhang 0`, `--texture none`, a pitch under 0.5)
without `--why "<reason that cites the concept image>"`, for example `--why "concept: black tiled roof on black timber walls"`.
Without a reason the tool refuses (CLI) or warns (library); with one it records the reason as a look note. "To fit the size
cap" is not a reason: shorten the walls. Forms with no eave by design (sawtooth, dome) are exempt automatically.

## Forms beyond a pitched plane

`--style cone | dome | onion | tiered | sawtooth` (or the presets above) build curved, stacked and glazed roofs:
`cone` (`pitch`, `lean`, `finial`, `dormer`), `dome`/`onion` (`drum`, `ribs`, finial; radius under 4 falls back to a cone),
`tiered` (`tiers`, `skirt`, `inset`, `band`, `pitches`), `sawtooth` (`bays`, `glaze`). `eave: upturned` lifts the corners of a
dutch gable or hip like a pagoda; `overhang` may be `{north, south, east, west}`; `maxHeight` caps the roof in courses (with no
explicit pitch the roof is capped at its ratio cap). `mcd render --closeups` includes a roof close-up tile so the texture is visible.
`examples/roofs/regression.png` shows the eight reference cases (`node examples/roofs/regression.mjs`).

`examples/roofs/presets.png` shows every preset on a small 9x7 shop and a 23x17 civic block
(`node examples/roofs/presets.mjs`).

## Styles (the raw options)

`examples/roofs/gallery.png` shows every style on the same L-plan house (`node examples/roofs/gallery.mjs`).

| style | what it is | good for |
|---|---|---|
| `gable` | two slopes per wing; ridges along each wing's long side, cross-gables meeting in valleys; gable walls filled with the wall block | cottages, barns, row houses (`ridgeAxis` to turn the ridge) |
| `hip` | slopes on every side; true hips (outer stairs) and valleys (inner stairs) on any rectilinear plan | villas, civic buildings, anything seen from all sides |
| `pyramid` | a hip that comes to points; a square plan gives a single peak | pavilions, towers |
| `mansard` | a steep lower slope (`pitch`, `lower` cells wide) under a shallow upper one (`upperPitch`, default half) | French or Second Empire roofs, a full storey in the roof, dormers |
| `gambrel` | gable wings with two pitches | barns, Dutch colonial |
| `flat-parapet` | a flat deck, a parapet (`parapet` courses) of the wall block, and slab coping | shops, offices, modern buildings |
| `shed` | one slope (the `low` side), with the high side walled | lean-tos, extensions, industrial buildings |
| `dutch-gable` | a hip with small gablets set back at the ridge ends (`inset`) | farmhouses, East Asian roofs |

## Options

- **`pitch`**:
  - `half`: slab steps, about 27°
  - `45`: stairs, 1:1
  - `steep`: stairs with full blocks, 2:1
  - `very-steep`: 3:1
  - or any number (rise per cell)

  Eaves never drop more than one course per cell, so a steep roof does not swallow the top of the wall.
- **`overhang`** 0–2 (default 1). **`eave`**:
  - `plain`
  - `flared`: a half-pitch kick at the eave
  - `cornice`: a course of upside-down `trim` stairs under the eave, with dentils of alternating `trim` blocks under that

  `soffit: true` (or a material) puts top slabs under a plain overhang.
- **Materials**:
  - `material` (the roof; any form of the name works: `deepslate_tiles`, `deepslate_tile`, `spruce`)
  - `trim` (cornice, dentils, tower band)
  - `gable` (the gable-end wall; default: the walls' own block)
  - `verge` (the barge course over each gable end)
  - `hips` (the hip stairs)
  - `pattern: {material, every, offset}` (banded courses)
- **`ridge`**:
  - `slab` (default for 45° and steeper): a half slab on the ridge
  - `wall`: a joined wall
  - `crest`: joined iron bars, the Victorian ridge crest
  - `rods`: end rods every other cell
  - `none`
  - or any block
- **`dormers`**: `{face, count | every, style: gable|shed|eyebrow, width (3), height (2), window, wall}`. Dormers are
  placed symmetrically on that face of the largest wing, keep clear of hip ends and the pediment, and step down or
  drop out where the main roof doesn't rise over them within four rows (so they never tunnel through it).
- **`pediment`**: `{face, width (55% of the face), pitch (45), tympanum, cornice (raking cornice material), oculus
  (true), depth}`, or just `"north"`. This is a classical cross-gable over the front half of that face, with its
  gable filled with `tympanum`, a raking cornice, and a small round window in the middle.
- **`chimneys`**: `[{at: [x,z], size, material, rise}]`. A chimney rises `rise` (2) above the roof top. A 1x1 chimney
  gets a smoking campfire on top, and bigger ones get slab caps.
- **`tower`**: `{at: [x,z], size (n or [w,d]), height (above the roof top), top: lantern|spire|cap, material}`. This
  is a hollow shaft through the roof with a band and small openings near the top, finished with one of:
  - `lantern`: corner posts, iron-bar railings, a hanging lantern, a small pyramid cap and a lightning-rod finial
  - `spire`: a 3:1 pyramid
  - `cap`: slab coping
- **`monitor`** (gable styles): a louvred vent along the middle 60% of the ridge. **`gableCornice`**: the cornice
  also runs across the gable ends (the base of a pediment). **`dentils: false`**: a slim cornice. **`rail`**
  (flat-parapet): iron bars along the coping.
- **`keep`**: `[{from:[x,y,z], to:[x,y,z]}]`, cells never written or removed (a chimney or tower you want to keep).
  Functional cells (redstone, doors and the rest) are always protected. `grow` (default true) grows the grid to fit
  overhangs and height; the result's `shift` says how far everything moved.

## Re-roofing an existing build

`reroof` and `mcd roof` work in three steps:
1. **Find the walls.** Tall columns are walls; the holes between them are filled to get the plan.
2. **Find the eave.** Each perimeter column's wall top is its highest solid with a mostly solid column beneath
   (stairs and slabs at the top count as roof). The eave is the most common wall top.
3. **Find the footprint.** Columns that reach the eave band form it, so a low porch drops out. It is cleaned up
   (one-cell notches filled, one-cell pilasters and buttresses dropped), split into rectangles, and keep boxes are
   cut out.

Then it removes everything above the eave over the footprint (+3 for old overhangs), plus old eave stairs and slabs,
and builds the style. Check `--detect` first. If the footprint is wrong, pass `--footprint x0,z0,x1,z1;...` and
`--y`.

## Choosing a roof that matches a concept

- **Roof height**: a steep hip over a 16-wide plan rises 16 blocks, which is taller than most concepts show. For
  "steep slate" on a wide building, use a **mansard** (`pitch: steep`, `lower: 3`): it reads as a steep roof from
  the street, and the shallow top holds the crest.
- **A front pediment** turns a plain roof into a civic one. Use `cornice` in an accent material (oak reads as gilt
  against slate) and `eave: cornice` on the main roof.
- **Towers** read best small. An elevator head is the shaft's front 4x5 and one storey above the roof, not the whole
  shaft.

The worked example is `examples/roofs/deepslate.mjs`, which re-roofs Deepslate Holdings to match its concept.
`examples/roofs/deepslate-compare.png` shows the concept, before and after.

# Build workflow (`mcd-agent build`, `mcd-agent revise`)

**Status: experimental.** One best-effort build per call, then revisions only when a person says what to change. In the
owner's blind picks (2026-10) this one-shot build beat stock Claude 8-0. It also beat both automatic improvement loops
tried before it: parallel Haiku fix-up tasks (4-1) and taste-profile revision rounds (3-0; the rounds pushed "fewer
colours, more weathering" and stripped the colour the owner liked), which cost 2-4x more.

A concept image is inspiration, not a fidelity target. The workflow is a typed BAML program (`baml_src/ns_workflow/`)
packed into one executable; the model work goes through `claude -p` on the user's Claude plan, the card through `mcd`.

| Command | Who | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| `build` | a Sonnet session with this plugin, then `mcd card` | `v1.nbt` and `v1.litematic` (the same build, for Litematica), `v1-card.png`, `elements.md` (recognisable elements), `gaps.md` (what the toolkit couldn't do), `build-report.json`, `summary.json` |
| `revise` | the same kind of session, in the same directory | applies ONE comment to the latest `vN.nbt`, leaving the rest alone: `vN+1.nbt`, its card, `vN+1-revise.json` (what was applied and skipped); `summary.json` points at it |

## Run it

```bash
A="node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/bin/mcd-agent.mjs"
$A build  --dir runs/tea-house --name tea-house --brief-file brief.txt [--concept concept.png]
$A revise --dir runs/tea-house --comment "warmer roof colour, and lanterns by the door"
$A build  --dir runs/castle --name castle --brief-file brief.txt --minutes 60 --sessions 4   # a big build
$A build  --dir runs/farm --name farm --brief-file brief.txt --lean                         # minimal spend
```

The brief is plain text: `BUILD: <name>: <what it is, its recognisable elements>.` plus `SIZE: about W wide (front, x),
D deep, H tall; 1:1 scale, a player is 2 blocks tall`. A comment is the user's own words: never write one for them.
Every model call is logged to `<dir>/ledger.jsonl` and summed into `summary.json` (`cost_usd`). In testing, a small revise
(two lanterns) took $0.26 and under 2 minutes.

## Read the result

`summary.json`: `kept` (the latest version), `best` (its `.nbt`), `litematic` (its `.litematic`), `card`, `summary` (what the build or the last revise
did), `revisions` (each comment with what was applied and skipped), `seconds`, `cost_usd`. Every version stays in the
run dir with its card, so a revise that misses can be compared and dropped.

**Big builds span sessions.** Each session works to a clock (`--minutes`: 45 for a build, 15 for a revise). The first
build session saves a whole first pass (massing and shell) by a third of the way in; every later save is a whole
building. With more than one session allowed, the first writes `plan.md` before building (every mass with block
coordinates, palette by role, one shared vocabulary of windows, caps and cornices, one generator module per part, a
checklist in order); every later session follows it and ticks it off, so the parts cohere. A session that can't finish answers `finished: false` with what is left, and the next session (up to
`--sessions`, default 2) continues from the files in the run dir: the generator scripts, `build.nbt`, `elements.md`,
and the transcripts. A fresh session also means a fresh context window, so size isn't capped by one session's memory.
`summary.json` says `finished` and how many `sessions` were used.

**Lean mode (`--lean`) is the minimal-spend setting.** One Sonnet session DESIGNS and writes no code (its output is
the scarce spend): `elements.md` (the required elements, each with its real construction) and `plan.md` (every mass
with block coordinates, the palette by role, the vocabulary of repeated elements and furniture, the interior, every
opening, the parts with their specs). A Haiku session then writes the kit from it: `palette.json` (ids checked),
`vocab.mjs` (the palette and a tested helper per vocabulary item), one stub module per part, and `make.sh` (the one
command that builds `build.nbt`, roof preset included). Then one Codex conversation (`tools/bin/codex-shim.mjs`, a BAML client on the
ChatGPT plan) draws concept art of the planned site from the planner's description and palette, and in the same turn
reports the prompt it used and the block palette it drew with (`concept.json`). That palette, with ids checked against
the game, becomes `palette.json`, so the workers build from the ids the picture was made of instead of guessing. A
`--concept` the user gave is used instead; without Codex there's no art and the planner's palette stands. `build.mjs` runs the parts through `runParts`: a later part can only add into
air (it can't break an earlier part's wall), and every off-palette block is reported; the art's palette adds to the
planner's, never shrinks it. After each part the workflow rebuilds and reads `parts-report.json`: a part that left
refused writes or off-palette blocks gets one short Haiku session to fix exactly those. Then the parts are built by short Haiku sessions (at most `--sessions` parts, default 6, of `--minutes`,
default 12), each filling in only its own module, running `make.sh`, checking, rendering and ticking the plan: the
first part (massing and shell) alone, then every other part AT ONCE, each in its own copy of the run (`crew/`), the whole
wave at once (`--crew`, default 24). The modules are merged back and rebuilt in plan order; parts that clash in the merge get parallel fix
sessions. Every room in the plan gets its own Haiku INTERIOR DESIGNER in that parallel wave (purpose, mood and key pieces
from the plan; the layout and furniture are theirs, kept walkable). Last, a Haiku INSPECTOR runs `mcd walk` (can a
player walk from the entrance into every room?) and renders the whole, fixing what fell between the parts.
`--planner <alias>` picks the planner's model (default sonnet); any model may carry an effort, e.g. `haiku@medium`
(the kit writer runs at medium: most of Haiku's output at high effort is thinking). The planner holds the design, the workers hold the labour. A lean revise is
Haiku, 10 minutes x 2. Models are the aliases (`haiku`, `sonnet`): always the latest. Rerunning a stopped lean build keeps its `plan.json` and `concept.png` instead of paying for
them again. **Plan once, build many:** after planning and art, the run keeps them pristine in `plan-kit/`, and

# Build workflow (`mcd-agent build`, `mcd-agent revise`)

**Status: experimental.** One best-effort build per call, then revisions only when a person says what to change. In the
owner's blind picks (2026-10) this one-shot build beat stock Claude 8-0. It also beat both automatic improvement loops
tried before it: parallel Haiku fix-up tasks (4-1) and taste-profile revision rounds (3-0; the rounds pushed "fewer
colours, more weathering" and stripped the colour the owner liked), which cost 2-4x more.

A concept image is inspiration, not a fidelity target. The workflow is a typed BAML program (`baml_src/ns_workflow/`)
packed into one executable; the model work goes through `claude -p` on the user's Claude plan, the card through `mcd`.

| Command | Who | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| `build` | a Sonnet session with this plugin, then `mcd card` | `v1.nbt` and `v1.litematic` (the same build, for Litematica), `v1-card.png`, `elements.md` (recognisable elements), `gaps.md` (what the toolkit couldn't do), `build-report.json`, `summary.json` |
| `revise` | the same kind of session, in the same directory | applies ONE comment to the latest `vN.nbt`, leaving the rest alone: `vN+1.nbt`, its card, `vN+1-revise.json` (what was applied and skipped); `summary.json` points at it |

## Run it

```bash
A="node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/bin/mcd-agent.mjs"
$A build  --dir runs/tea-house --name tea-house --brief-file brief.txt [--concept concept.png]
$A revise --dir runs/tea-house --comment "warmer roof colour, and lanterns by the door"
$A build  --dir runs/castle --name castle --brief-file brief.txt --minutes 60 --sessions 4   # a big build
$A build  --dir runs/farm --name farm --brief-file brief.txt --lean                         # minimal spend
```

The brief is plain text: `BUILD: <name>: <what it is, its recognisable elements>.` plus `SIZE: about W wide (front, x),
D deep, H tall; 1:1 scale, a player is 2 blocks tall`. A comment is the user's own words: never write one for them.
Every model call is logged to `<dir>/ledger.jsonl` and summed into `summary.json` (`cost_usd`). In testing, a small revise
(two lanterns) took $0.26 and under 2 minutes.

## Read the result

`summary.json`: `kept` (the latest version), `best` (its `.nbt`), `litematic` (its `.litematic`), `card`, `summary` (what the build or the last revise
did), `revisions` (each comment with what was applied and skipped), `seconds`, `cost_usd`. Every version stays in the
run dir with its card, so a revise that misses can be compared and dropped.

**Big builds span sessions.** Each session works to a clock (`--minutes`: 45 for a build, 15 for a revise). The first
build session saves a whole first pass (massing and shell) by a third of the way in; every later save is a whole
building. With more than one session allowed, the first writes `plan.md` before building (every mass with block
coordinates, palette by role, one shared vocabulary of windows, caps and cornices, one generator module per part, a
checklist in order); every later session follows it and ticks it off, so the parts cohere. A session that can't finish answers `finished: false` with what is left, and the next session (up to
`--sessions`, default 2) continues from the files in the run dir: the generator scripts, `build.nbt`, `elements.md`,
and the transcripts. A fresh session also means a fresh context window, so size isn't capped by one session's memory.
`summary.json` says `finished` and how many `sessions` were used.

**Lean mode (`--lean`) is the minimal-spend setting.** One Sonnet session DESIGNS and writes no code (its output is
the scarce spend): `elements.md` (the required elements, each with its real construction) and `plan.md` (every mass
with block coordinates, the palette by role, the vocabulary of repeated elements and furniture, the interior, every
opening, the parts with their specs). A Haiku session then writes the kit from it: `palette.json` (ids checked),
`vocab.mjs` (the palette and a tested helper per vocabulary item), one stub module per part, and `make.sh` (the one
command that builds `build.nbt`, roof preset included). Then one Codex conversation (`tools/bin/codex-shim.mjs`, a BAML client on the
ChatGPT plan) draws concept art of the planned site from the planner's description and palette, and in the same turn
reports the prompt it used and the block palette it drew with (`concept.json`). That palette, with ids checked against
the game, becomes `palette.json`, so the workers build from the ids the picture was made of instead of guessing. A
`--concept` the user gave is used instead; without Codex there's no art and the planner's palette stands. `build.mjs` runs the parts through `runParts`: a later part can only add into
air (it can't break an earlier part's wall), and every off-palette block is reported; the art's palette adds to the
planner's, never shrinks it. After each part the workflow rebuilds and reads `parts-report.json`: a part that left
refused writes or off-palette blocks gets one short Haiku session to fix exactly those. Then the parts are built by short Haiku sessions (at most `--sessions` parts, default 6, of `--minutes`,
default 12), each filling in only its own module, running `make.sh`, checking, rendering and ticking the plan: the
first part (massing and shell) alone, then every other part AT ONCE, each in its own copy of the run (`crew/`), the whole
wave at once (`--crew`, default 24). The modules are merged back and rebuilt in plan order; parts that clash in the merge get parallel fix
sessions. Every room in the plan gets its own Haiku INTERIOR DESIGNER in that parallel wave (purpose, mood and key pieces
from the plan; the layout and furniture are theirs, kept walkable). Last, a Haiku INSPECTOR runs `mcd walk` (can a
player walk from the entrance into every room?) and renders the whole, fixing what fell between the parts.
`--planner <alias>` picks the planner's model (default sonnet); any model may carry an effort, e.g. `haiku@medium`
(the kit writer runs at medium: most of Haiku's output at high effort is thinking). The planner holds the design, the workers hold the labour. A lean revise is
Haiku, 10 minutes x 2. Models are the aliases (`haiku`, `sonnet`): always the latest. Rerunning a stopped lean build keeps its `plan.json` and `concept.png` instead of paying for
them again. **Plan once, build many:** after planning and art, the run keeps them pristine in `plan-kit/`, and
`build --from-plan <that run> --dir <new run>` starts another Haiku crew from it with no planner or art cost (for
variants to pick from, or a retry). `--model <id>` picks any other builder model.

**Nothing is lost if a session overruns.** The hard limit is 15 minutes past the clock. A session cut off there keeps
its last `build.nbt`, the next session is told it was cut off and where its transcript is, `sessions/*.jsonl` holds
every session's full transcript, and the ledger gets a row with its tokens (`cost: null`, `stopped`). A watchdog stops

# Plan: Roman domus (villa urbana) "villa-sonnet"

Identity: a single-storey Pompeian town house on a street, windowless to the street except four shuttered shops and a recessed entrance
(fauces) in the middle; behind it the atrium (open to the sky, rain pool), the tablinum on the same axis, and a peristyle garden with a
white colonnade, fountain, statues and clipped hedges. Cream plaster, red dado, red-tile roofs sloping into the courts, bronze lamps.
Site x 0..35 (36), z 0..47 (48), y 0..9 (ridges; one chimney may reach y10). Front = NORTH (-z), street at z<0.
Ground y=0. HOUSE FLOOR y=1 (podium), so inside a player stands at y=2. All ranges inclusive. Mirror rule: x' = 35 - x (axis between x17|x18).
Workers: read `vocab.mjs` first, then only your own part file. `make.sh` rebuilds everything. Later parts only ADD into air: a part never
writes into a cell an earlier part filled; P1 therefore leaves every opening (and every cell listed "left to Pn") unset.
HARD RULE: nothing but P2 (roofs) stands at y>=7 inside x0..35, z2..45. Walls/columns/ceilings stop at y=6.

## SITE (masses)
| mass | x | y | z | notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| street + sidewalk | 0..35 | 0 | 0..1 | `andesite`/`polished_andesite` hash; kerb row at z=0 (P3) |
| rear lane | 0..35 | 0 | 46..47 | `gravel` 70 / `dirt_path` 30 (P6) |
| foundation | 0..35 | 0 | 2..45 | P1: `stone_bricks`; garden court x11..24,z35..41 = `dirt`; pool x15..20,z14..17 = `blue_terracotta` |
| floor layer | 0..35 | 1 | 2..45 | P1: per-room mosaic/floor (ROOMS); NOT laid at: garden court x11..24,z35..41; pool x15..20,z14..17 (left to P5/P4) |
| outer walls | | 1..6 | z=2, z=45, x=0, x=35 | wallCell roles; ceiling plane y=6 |
| front block (4 shops + fauces) | 0..35 | 2..6 | 2..9 | depth: wall z2, rooms z3..8, wall z9 |
| atrium block | 0..35 | 2..6 | 10..21 | atrium x10..25; cubicula W x1..8, E x27..34 |
| tablinum block | 0..35 | 2..6 | 22..31 | kitchen x1..9, tablinum x11..24, triclinium x26..34 |
| peristyle block | 0..35 | 2..6 | 32..45 | rooms x1..5 / x30..34, ring walkway x7..28, court x11..24,z35..41 |
| compluvium (open) | 14..21 | 6..9 | 13..18 | hole in ceiling and roof |
| garden court (open) | 11..24 | 1..9 | 35..41 | open sky |
| roofs | 0..35 | 7..9 | 2..45 | 16 pieces (table below), `red-tile` palette |

### Roof pieces (P2). Preset base: `temple` (red-tile palette, low pitch, quartz raking cornice) with these overrides per piece (pitch half; roof sits on wall top y6 so first roof course is y7; ridge max y9). Chosen by building type: Mediterranean colonnaded house -> `temple` preset (red-tile), not `cottage`.

| R6 atrium S | 14..25, 19..21 | shed | low = north | |
| R7 atrium W | 10..13, 13..21 | shed | low = east | pinwheel: R4..R7 do not overlap, hole x14..21,z13..18 stays open |
| R8 kitchen | 0..9, 22..31 | gable | ridge along z (x=4..5) | chimney E31 |
| R9 tablinum | 10..25, 22..31 | gable | ridge along x (z=26..27) | |
| R10 triclinium | 26..35, 22..31 | gable | ridge along z (x=30..31) | |

Roof pieces must not roof the open holes: compluvium x14..21,z13..18 and garden x11..24,z35..41.

Contrast: cream walls vs red tile roof vs red dado vs white marble vs dark-oak/spruce wood vs bronze. Quartz columns pop against the red dado/cream.

## PARTS (each a 12-minute job; order = build order)
1. P1 `parts/shell.mjs` - MASSING AND SHELL. Foundation y0 (stone_bricks; dirt under the garden; `blue_terracotta` under the pool), floor y1 laid per ROOMS (mosaic helper; not at the garden court / pool cells), every wall line with its openings left unset (wallLine, ROOMS/OPENINGS lists), outer walls, fauces side walls, pilasters at (15,z2),(20,z2) (`pilaster`), ceiling y6 `spruce_planks` over every room, the ring walkways, with the holes listed (compluvium, garden court, flue (2,6,26)), y6 cornice. Ticks E1, E2 (walls), E5 (rooms), E7 (ceiling hole), E10, E11 (court void), E19, E21, E22, E23, E26 (opening).
2. P2 `parts/roofs.mjs` - ROOFS. All 16 pieces in the table, via `mcd roof` / `roof()` with preset `temple` + overrides, dry-run first; compluvium and garden holes open; pediment (E30); kitchen chimney stack (E31). Ticks E20, E30, E31.
3. P3 `parts/street.mjs` - STREET FRONT. Sidewalk, kerb, step, fauces doors + fanlight + lintel row, shopWindow counters and pots, shutters, lampstands and pots on the sidewalk. Ticks E3, E4, E5 (counters), E6, E29.
4. P4 `parts/atrium.mjs` - ATRIUM + INTERIOR JOINERY. Impluvium water and coping, tuscanColumn x4, dark-oak edge beams, atrium niches/statues (11,12),(24,12), pilasters framing atrium/tablinum/fauces openings, ALL interior `doorway`s on the OPENINGS table marked P4, atrium hangLamps and corner pots. Ticks E7 (beams), E8, E9, E10 (pilasters), E16 (niches), E24 (atrium lamps), E25 (atrium pots).
5. P5 `parts/peristyle.mjs` - PERISTYLE GARDEN. 18 columns, architrave y6, stylobate, garden ground, gravel ring, beds with hedges and flowers, fountain, 4 statues, benches, doorways on x=6/x=29, pilasters at z=31 (x14,x21), colonnade hangLamps. Ticks E11..E16, E12, E24 (colonnade lamps).
6. P6 `parts/finish.mjs` - FINISH. Window grilles on all x=0/x=35/z=45 windows, rear door pair and rear lane, back-wall windows, remaining lampstands and pots, final look: render from the street, down the axis (`--eye 17.5,3.6,0 --look 17.5,3.6,40`), and from above. Ticks E24, E25, E26, E28, E27 (shell only).

- [x] P1 shell  - [ ] P2 roofs  - [ ] P3 street  - [ ] P4 atrium  - [ ] P5 peristyle  - [ ] P6 finish

## NOTES for workers
- Windows line up with rooms: shop windows with shops, x=0/x=35 windows with the rooms named in ROOMS.
- Doors: `spruce_door` facing = the side the door faces when closed, open them (`open=true`) in the fauces so the player walks in; interior doorways may stay closed (inspector walk treats a door as passable) but prefer open=true for the inspector.
- Water: the pool (x15..20,z14..17) and fountain (x16..19,z37..39) are the only water; both are enclosed below and on all four sides by non-air blocks. `water_cauldron` is not a water source: it is just a block.
- The roof tool strips y>=7 in its footprint: run it once, after P1. Nothing else may exceed y6 in the house footprint (statues reach y5; chimney is P2's).
- Mirror everything with x' = 35 - x; asymmetric items: none, except the lararium (C6, SW) vs storeroom (C8, SE).
- Room designers: floors and walls are done; place furniture only on y2.. in air, keep a 1-wide walkable line from each door to the room's centre, never in a doorway cell or a window cell.
- P1 (shell) built: foundation y0, floors y1 per ROOMS, wall lines y1..6 with every OPENINGS cell air (interior doorways at y2..3 too), fauces pilasters + smooth_quartz lintel (x16..19, y6, z2), spruce ceiling y6 with the compluvium, garden court and flue holes. Elements touched by P1: E1, E2, E5, E7 (hole), E10, E11 (court void), E19 (room shell), E21, E22, E23, E26 (opening). P1 additions/simplifications: solid z=38 gap walls at x1..5 and x30..34 (between C5/C6 and C7/C8, not in the PARTS list); triclinium border depth-1 ring is `red_terracotta` (the meander is not built); garden court and column stylobate cells at y1 left unset for P5.
- CONFLICT for P4/P5: P1's wall lines already occupy y2..6 at the pilaster cells (15,9),(20,9),(14,22),(21,22),(14,31),(21,31) as plaster, so those pilaster writes will be REFUSED by runParts. Decide in P4/P5 whether to keep the plaster or to write the pilasters there (P1 cannot leave them air without opening the wall).

# Plan: suburban McMansion "mcmansion-opus-medium"

Identity: a 2000s cul-de-sac McMansion: a two-storey beige box made "grand" by a jumble of parts on the street face: a tall white-trimmed
front gable over a double-height columned portico, an octagonal turret bay with a cone at the west corner, a three-car garage wing set
back on the east, grey stone veneer on the lower front, birch-beige siding everywhere else, white belt/plate/quoins, black shutters,
dark slate-grey asphalt hips, a big stone chimney on the west end. Wide concrete drive, clipped lawn, shrubs, one young birch, a back deck.
Site x 0..43, z 0..31, y 0..17. Front = NORTH (z0 = cul-de-sac road). Ground y0. HOUSE FLOOR y1 (stand y2), ground storey air y2..4,
upper floor y5 (stand y6), upper air y6..8, ceiling + wall plate y9, roofs y10+. GARAGE floor y0, air y1..4, bonus floor y5.
All ranges inclusive. Later parts only ADD into air: every opening and reserved cell below is left AIR by P1.
HARD RULE: in the house footprint nothing but P2 (roofs) and the turret walls (y10..11) / chimney stack stands at y>=10.

## SITE (masses)
| mass | x | y | z | notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| road | 0..43 | 0 | 0 | `gray_concrete` (P5) |
| sidewalk | 0..43 | 0 | 1 | `light_gray_concrete`; driveway crossing x29..41 = `smooth_stone` (P5) |
| driveway | 29..41 | 0 | 2..12 | `smooth_stone` (P5); flares 1 cell at z2: x28 and x42 `smooth_stone` |
| front lawn | 0..28 | 0 | 2..10 | `grass_block` except walk/beds/porch (P5) |
| side yards | 0..1, 42..43 | 0 | 2..31 | grass (chimney stands at x0..1 z20..23) |
| back yard | 0..43 | 0 | 26..31 | grass; deck x6..24 z26..30 |
| foundation | 2..29 (+turret, entry) | 0 | 7..25 | P1 `stone_bricks` under the house; garage x29..41 z13..25 y0 = `smooth_stone` floor |
| main block | 2..29 | 1..9 | 11..25 | 2 storeys; walls x2, x29, z11, z25 |
| entry projection | 12..21 | 1..9 | 9..10 | front wall z9, sides x12/x21 at z10; main wall z11 omitted x13..20 at y2..8 |
| portico | 11..22 | 1..9 | 4..8 | open: floor y1 z5..8, steps z4, 4 columns z5, entablature y9 (P3) |
| turret bay | 2..7 | 1..11 | 7..11 | octagon: front z7 x3..6; chamfer cells (2,8),(7,8); sides x2,x7 at z9..10; back = main wall z11 (raised to y11 for x2..7) |
| garage wing | 29..41 | 0..9 | 13..25 | walls x29 (shared), x41, z13, z25; 3 door openings in z13 |
| chimney | 0..1 | 0..15 | 20..23 | stone stack outside wall x2 (P1) |
| roofs | 1..42 | 10..17 | 4..26 | P2, table below |
| back deck | 5..24 | 1..2 | 26..30 | P5 |

### Roofs (P2). Building type: a hipped suburban house with a classical front gable → preset `civic` (45° hip, `slate` palette, quartz dentil
cornice, quartz front pediment); a plain house would be `cottage`, but a McMansion's signature is hips + a pedimented front gable. Overrides:
| call | footprint rects [x0,z0,x1,z1] (R0 FIRST) | options |
|---|---|---|
| R-main | [[4,11,29,25],[2,11,3,25],[29,13,41,25],[11,5,22,10]] | `roof(g, rects, "civic", { y:10, style:"hip", pitch:0.6, overhang:1, material:"slate", eave:"cornice", trim:"smooth_quartz", ridge:"slab", pediment:{face:"north", width:12, pitch:1.25, tympanum:"birch_planks", cornice:"smooth_quartz", oculus:true}, dormers:{face:"south", count:2, style:"gable", width:3, height:2, window:"glass_pane", wall:"birch_planks"}, keep:[{from:[1,10,6],to:[8,30,11]} /*turret*/, {from:[0,0,19],to:[1,30,24]} /*chimney*/] })` |
| R-turret | [[2,7,7,11]] | after R-main: `roof(g, rects, "cone", { y:12, material:"slate", maxHeight:5, finial:true, overhang:1 })`; if the tool's finial is not a rod, add `lightning_rod` on the apex |
Targets (dry-run first, adjust `pitch` only): main hip ridge/deck ≤ y14; pediment peak y15..16 = the tallest roof; turret apex y16..17.
R0 = [4,11,29,25] is chosen so the pediment centres on x16.5 = the entry axis (x11..22). Check the render: if the pediment's front
triangle at z5 is left open, fill the tympanum at z5 with `birch_planks` + the half-round window of E10 (cells inside the rake only).

## PALETTE (all ids checked with `mcd blocks --check`; `chain` is `iron_chain`; `painting` is an entity: not used)
| role | blocks | where / share |
|---|---|---|
| siding (55%) | `birch_planks`, `birch_slab`, `birch_stairs`, `birch_fence`, `birch_door`, `birch_trapdoor` | walls above the veneer, all sides/back; interior partitions |
| stone veneer (15%) | `stone_bricks` 45 / `andesite` 25 / `tuff_bricks` 20 / `cobblestone` 10 (hash (x*7+y*5+z*13)%20), `stone_brick_stairs`, `stone_brick_slab`, `stone_brick_wall`, `chiseled_stone_bricks` | front faces y1..4, chimney, plinth y1, foundation |
| white trim (10%) | `smooth_quartz`, `quartz_block`, `quartz_pillar`, `chiseled_quartz_block`, `quartz_bricks`, `quartz_stairs`, `quartz_slab`, `smooth_quartz_slab`, `smooth_quartz_stairs` | belt y5, plate y9, quoins, columns, arches, sills, casings, cornice |
| roof (15%) | `slate` palette: `cobbled_deepslate`, `deepslate_tiles`, `polished_deepslate`, `deepslate_tile_stairs`, `deepslate_tile_slab`, `blackstone_bricks` eave | all roofs |
| black accents | `dark_oak_trapdoor` (shutters), `dark_oak_door`, `dark_oak_planks`, `dark_oak_stairs`, `dark_oak_slab`, `dark_oak_fence` | shutters, front/back doors, stair |
| garage doors | `spruce_trapdoor`, `glass_pane` | carriage doors |
| glass | `glass_pane`, `glass` | windows |
| floors | `oak_planks` (hardwood), `polished_diorite` + `smooth_quartz` (marble), `smooth_stone` (garage, kitchen tile alt), `polished_andesite` (mudroom), `white_concrete` (bath), carpets `white_carpet`, `light_gray_carpet` | ROOMS |
| ground | `grass_block`, `podzol` (mulch), `smooth_stone`, `bricks`, `gray_concrete`, `light_gray_concrete`, `dirt_path` | site |
| plants | `azalea_leaves`, `flowering_azalea_leaves`, `birch_log`, `birch_leaves`, `white_tulip`, `red_tulip`, `peony`, `rose_bush`, `lilac`, `short_grass`, `potted_fern`, `flower_pot` | beds, tree |
| deck | `spruce_planks`, `spruce_fence`, `spruce_stairs`, `spruce_slab`, `spruce_pressure_plate` | deck |

A beige-birch, stone-veneered two-storey McMansion (x2..41, z5..25 on a 44x32 lot): a double-height 4-column portico under a tall quartz-trimmed front pediment (centred on x16.5), an octagonal turret bay with a cone at the west corner, and a set-back three-car garage wing with carriage doors, all under one slate hip roof (pitch 0.6, south dormers). input.concept_subject: A big beige suburban McMansion on a cul-de-sac lot, seen from the street (north). The centrepiece is a tall white-trimmed front gable over a double-height portico: four white quartz columns, a dark double front door with glass sidelights and an arched fanlight, a large arched Palladian window above it, and a half-round window in the birch-beige gable. To the west is an octagonal two-storey turret bay with a slate cone roof and a rod finial. A big grey stone chimney rises up the west end wall. To the east is a three-car garage wing, set back two blocks, with three dark spruce carriage doors with glass top lites, white headers, lanterns on the stone piers, and a bonus room above with small shuttered windows. The lower front is grey stone veneer up to a white belt course; above it, and on every other wall, is pale beige birch siding with a white top plate and paired white quoins. Tall 2-wide arched windows have white sills and black shutters. Everything sits under one jumbled dark slate-grey asphalt hip roof with a white dentil cornice, gable dormers at the back, and the front gable and turret cone poking above. In front: a wide pale concrete driveway, a brick walk to the portico steps, lamp posts, a mailbox, a clipped green lawn with mulched beds of round shrubs and tulips along the foundation, and one young birch. Behind: a spruce deck with a railing, a grill and a patio table.

input.concept_palette: birch planks (beige siding); stone bricks, andesite, tuff bricks, cobblestone (stone veneer, chimney); smooth quartz, quartz pillar, quartz bricks, quartz stairs and slabs (white trim, columns, quoins); cobbled deepslate, deepslate tiles, polished deepslate, blackstone bricks (slate asphalt roof); dark oak trapdoors and doors (black shutters, front door); spruce trapdoors and glass panes (carriage doors); glass panes; smooth stone (driveway); bricks (walk); grass block, podzol mulch, azalea leaves, birch log and leaves; spruce planks and fence (deck); lanterns

structured_output.summary:
A beige-birch, stone-veneered two-storey McMansion (x2..41, z5..25 on a 44x32 lot): a double-height 4-column portico under a tall quartz-trimmed front pediment (centred on x16.5), an octagonal turret bay with a cone at the west corner, and a set-back three-car garage wing with carriage doors, all under one slate hip roof (pitch 0.6, south dormers). There's a big stone chimney on the west end, arched windows with black shutters, a wide concrete drive, lawn with shrubs and a young birch, and a back deck.
Inside: a double-height foyer with a sweeping stair and gallery, office, dining room, open kitchen/family room with a fireplace, and a mudroom on the ground floor; upstairs a primary suite (bedroom, walk-in closet, bath), three bedrooms and a bonus room over the garage.
